EN: An orbit is sometimes described as "falling and missing the ground." In the context of space travel it's \nthe way one object goes around another in space, and here it is about getting your vessel to travel \naround a body.

The gravity of Kerbin attracts the 
spaceship in a curving path. 

Your vessel needs to be moving 
at just the right velocity to stay in 
orbit (as opposed to escaping, or 
worse, crashing).
The most basic goal of any Kerbin-based space program is to get into orbit and return back to Kerbin.
Once you reach the target altitude, you need to burn prograde to increase \nyour velocity. You burn until you are fast enough to stay in orbit.
The gravity turn ascent will get you to orbital height, but it's not enough to keep you up there.

The point on an orbit furthest\nfrom the object you are orbiting.

Note: the color gradient of the orbit line shows the direction of rotation.
Orbiting the planet in the same \ndirection as its rotation direction \nis a prograde orbit.
Inclination is the angle an orbit \ndiffers from the equator of\nthe object its orbiting.
Orbits are described as prograde \nor retrograde relative to the \nplanet's rotation.
There are six directions when looking at a spaceship. These directions are relative to \nthe orbit of the ship, so they will "move" as you burn or when you change Sphere of \nInfluence (SOI).
You can see their symbols and directions\nin relation to this satellite below.
Orbit eccentricity describes how far from a circular orbit you are.

Without knowing how an orbit is described you might find it hard to get a vessel to the right destination \nin space. That's why it is important to understand the components of an orbit that will help you on the \nway to a successful space program.
In this section the parts of orbits, and orbital mechanics, that will help you to shoot for the stars will be \nexplained (and maybe even some of the mathematics involved).
Normal / Anti-Normal are the directions at 90 degrees to the current path of travel, perpendicular to the \norbit's plane.
Burning in the anti-normal direction pushes\nyour future orbit to the "South."
Side view of Kerbin - Orbit direction (prograde) can be seen from gradient.
Burning in the normal direction pushes your\nfuture orbit to the "North."

Thinking in simple straight lines, a vessel that is at 0m/s requires a change in velocity of 200m/s, a Δv of \n200m/s. To slow the vessel (because there are no brakes in space) we need to add more velocity, but in \nthe other direction. So to reach 100m/s we require another Δv of 100m/s.
